messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Authority Presence: Police
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
Thomas is a thirty-five-year-old special education teacher who has been on medical leave for the past six weeks. He came to therapy at the urging of his school principal, who noticed he had stopped returning emails and had missed three consecutive staff meetings without explanation. What Thomas himself described, in a quiet and halting voice, was a feeling that he had been broken by something that should not have broken him.

The event itself happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late November. Thomas had stayed late at school to finish a behavior intervention plan for a non-verbal student named Marcus, a boy who communicated through picture cards and whose outbursts Thomas had learned to read like a second language. By the time he walked to his car, the parking lot was nearly empty. Two men came from behind the dumpster near the gymnasium. One had a knife. They took his wallet, his phone, and the lanyard with his school keys. They told him to get on the ground. He did. The one with the knife pressed the blade against the back of his neck and told him not to look up. Thomas lay face-down on the cold asphalt, his cheek pressed against a discarded juice box, and listened to their footsteps fade. He was not physically injured beyond a scrape on his chin, but for weeks afterward his neck ached where the blade had been. The police arrived, took a report, and never found the men. Thomas thanked them, went home, and told himself he was fine.

He was not fine. The memory did not fade or blur. Instead it stayed in his mind like a series of photographs, each one perfectly clear: the fluorescent light of the parking lot, the crack in the asphalt near his left eye, the silver glint of the blade, the exact pattern of the sneakers worn by the man who stood over him. He could bring up any one of these images at will, and they would arrive fully formed, as if he were looking at them on a screen. What came with them, every time, was a surge of rage so sudden and hot that it frightened him. He would be standing at the kitchen counter making coffee and the image of the sneakers would appear, and his hands would shake and his jaw would clench and he would want to hurt someone. And then, just as quickly, the rage would curdle into guilt. He had done exactly what the men told him to do. He had lain down. He had not fought. He had not protected himself. He had gotten into that situation in the first place because he had not been paying attention, because he had been thinking about Marcus’s picture cards instead of scanning the parking lot like a competent adult. Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, he told himself. Somebody else would have seen them coming. Somebody else would have run, or fought, or done something. He had done nothing, and that made him inadequate.

Over the following months, Thomas began to change in ways he did not fully recognize until they had already taken hold. He could not relax, even in places he knew were safe. Sitting in his own living room, he would catch himself listening for footsteps. At the grocery store, he would notice the position of every exit the moment he walked through the door, and he would position his shopping cart so that he could see the entrance at all times. He started avoiding the school parking lot entirely, arriving an hour early so that he could park directly under a light and leave before any other staff member. When a colleague shouted across the hallway to get his attention, Thomas’s entire body would lock up, his heart hammering, before he could register that it was just a friendly voice. The worst trigger, unexpectedly, was the police. He saw a patrol car in his rearview mirror one morning and felt the same helplessness he had felt on the ground, the same certainty that something terrible was about to happen, even though he had done nothing wrong. He began taking side streets to avoid the main road where police cruisers parked.

The consequence that finally brought him to a therapist’s office was occupational. He had always been patient with Marcus, able to wait through the boy’s screaming episodes without flinching. But after the mugging, the shouting triggered something visceral. When Marcus began to yell in the classroom one afternoon, Thomas felt the rage rise in his chest, unbidden and terrifying. He had to leave the room. He stood in the hallway, shaking, and realized he could no longer do his job. He took medical leave the next day. In the weeks since, he has stayed mostly in his apartment. He scans the exits of every room he enters, including his own bedroom. He is certain that he is inadequate, that he failed the one test that mattered, and that he will never feel safe again. What he told me, at the end of our first session, was that he wanted to go back to work. But he was afraid that if he did, he would not be able to stay in the room.
